clue.text: Decline a long story

parts.note: a market or a mattress that declines sags
the article taken down exactly as it stands

explanation.surface: Somebody turning down the offer of a very long tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decline' wants to be the verb the sentence is built on; it is the drooping sense, what a shelf does under weight. Saga is Old Norse, the name of the Icelandic prose tales, and length is built into the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A saga is a long rambling narrative, the Icelandic epics having given their name to any story that goes on and on.

clue.text: Wears underwear twisted in the middle in drinking spots

indicators.note: Something twisted in the middle has its centre wrung round the other way, so the two letters at the heart of the word change places.

parts.note: to sport a hat or a moustache is to wear it about the place
bras are underwear, and their middle pair of letters has been turned round

explanation.surface: Going about in underclothes that have twisted themselves round, out among the pubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wears' reads as the verb holding the sentence up and is six letters of the answer outright. A sports bar is the kind of pub built round the televised match, American in origin and now on most British high streets.
explanation.definitionFit: A sports bar is a pub with the game on every screen, so it is one of the spots people go to for a drink.

clue.text: In Kigali, dancing with curt rocker's flourish

indicators.note: Letters set dancing are up on their feet and moving about, so they will not come down in the order they were printed in.

parts.note: the capital of Rwanda, six letters of raw material
four more letters joining the shuffle, ten in all

explanation.surface: A night's dancing in Rwanda's capital beside a brusque rock musician showing off.
explanation.walkthrough: Kigali is the capital of Rwanda, which is what lets the clue pose as a travel note. A lick is the short showy run of notes a guitarist drops into a song, the bit an air guitarist mimes.
explanation.definitionFit: A lick is the brief flashy phrase a guitarist throws in for effect, which is a rock player's flourish.

clue.text: Prepare what may be toast for deceased?

definitions.note: The answer is a noun phrase and 'deceased' an adjective, but in rhyming slang it is only ever used adjectivally — he's brown bread.

parts.note: to brown an onion is to give it its first turn in the pan, which is preparing it
toast is bread that has been under the grill

explanation.surface: Making toast, perhaps, for somebody who has died.
explanation.walkthrough: Brown bread rhymes with dead and is Cockney rhyming slang for it, which is what the question mark is owning. 'Toast' carries the same idea in its own slang sense of done for, so the clue points the same way twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Brown bread rhymes with dead, and in Cockney rhyming slang it is the everyday way of saying somebody has died.

clue.text: Stagger and feel sick audibly: it's the booze

indicators.note: What is audible is taken in by ear, so the words are wanted as they sound rather than as they are spelt.

parts.note: to reel is to stagger, and the two spellings come out of the mouth alike
to ail is to be unwell, and said aloud it is the drink

explanation.surface: Lurching about and queasy with it, and the drink is to blame.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface admits its own cause, which is why nothing in it looks like a definition until the colon. Real ale is beer left to condition in the cask, the cause the Campaign for Real Ale has fought for since 1971.
explanation.definitionFit: Real ale is cask-conditioned beer, so it is booze in the plainest sense — exactly what has the clue's drinker staggering.

clue.text: Claret? Flipping claret!?

definitions.note: Claret names the colour as well as the wine, and colour words in English sit either side of the noun — a claret shirt, a wine-red shirt.

indicators.note: To flip a thing is to turn it over end for end, so the two words it labels trade places.

parts.note: claret is the English name for the red wine of Bordeaux, and the pair of words is turned round

explanation.surface: A drinker spluttering at the claret he has just been handed.
explanation.walkthrough: The turn is of the two words, not of the letters, which is rarer than the usual mirror. 'Flipping' is also the mild oath the exasperation needs, and the exclamation mark is there to sell it.
explanation.definitionFit: Wine-red is the deep colour of red wine, and claret is that shade exactly — the colour took its name from the Bordeaux in the glass.

clue.text: Sci-fi film: drunken lunar bender

indicators.note: A drunken walk wanders off the line it set out on, and letters called drunken wander out of their printed order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

explanation.surface: A wild drinking spree held up on the moon.
explanation.walkthrough: A bender is British slang for a long session on the drink, so the fodder and its indicator tell one story between them. Ridley Scott's 1982 film takes its title from the police who hunt escaped replicants.
explanation.definitionFit: Blade Runner is Ridley Scott's 1982 film of a rainy future Los Angeles, so the definition names the genre it belongs to.

clue.text: Volcano regularly lost heat and area

indicators.note: To lose letters regularly is to shed every other one, so what is left of the run beside it is the second letter, the fourth and the sixth.

parts.note: every other letter of the two words together, counting from the second
a is the standard abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A volcano steadily losing both its heat and its spread.
explanation.walkthrough: The count runs straight through the gap between two words, which is what hides it — the space is no barrier to a letter-picking instruction. Etna stands above Catania in Sicily and is the largest active volcano in Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: Etna is the Sicilian mountain that has been erupting throughout recorded history, so the bare 'volcano' names it by example.

clue.text: Legendary queen performed at Globe

parts.note: did is the past of do, and an act that is done is performed
a globe is a sphere, and the round letter is the crossword's drawing of one

explanation.surface: A famous queen who once trod the boards at the Globe.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's playhouse is what the capital G offers, and the prologue to Henry V calls that theatre a wooden O. Dido is the queen of Carthage in Virgil's Aeneid, who kills herself when Aeneas sails away.
explanation.definitionFit: Dido is the Carthaginian queen of the Aeneid, a figure of legend rather than of record.

clue.text: Loves to embrace welcome somewhere in America

indicators.note: To embrace is to take into your arms, so the letters named first close round the ones named next.

parts.note: a love in tennis is a score of nothing, written as the round letter, and the clue asks for two
hi is the shortest welcome there is

explanation.surface: Someone who loves a hug greeting a friend out in the States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loves' looks like the verb of the sentence and is a pair of tennis zeros. The state takes its name from the river, an Iroquois word for good river.
explanation.definitionFit: Ohio is a state of the American Midwest, so the vague 'somewhere in America' is a definition by example.

clue.text: Kept in diamanté purses

indicators.note: To purse the lips is to pucker them out of shape, and letters puckered like that will not stay in the order given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters, the accent counting for nothing

explanation.surface: Something stored away in little handbags covered in imitation jewels.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics are the paper's mark for a word borrowed from French, and here they sit on the fodder rather than on anything foreign in the answer. 'Purses' reads as the bags and works as the verb for puckering.
explanation.definitionFit: To maintain a road or a house is to keep it in working order, so 'kept' is the plain past-tense synonym.

clue.text: Tear off with rare bird: it prevents a sale

indicators.note: Milk that has gone off is no longer what it was, and letters called off have stopped being the word they came from.

parts.note: four letters of fodder
eight more letters, twelve in all

explanation.surface: Rushing off in the company of an unusual bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear off' reads as one phrase meaning to dash away, and only the first word of it is material. A trade barrier is a tariff or a quota a government puts up to keep foreign goods out.
explanation.definitionFit: A trade barrier is the tariff or quota that stops goods at a border, so it is precisely the thing that keeps a sale from going through.

clue.text: E China, golden place where contrary views unheard?

parts.note: E is Echo in the radio alphabet, the word a pilot says for the letter
Ch is the two-letter label dictionaries put on China and things Chinese
amber is the golden yellow of fossil resin and of the middle traffic light

explanation.surface: A golden spot somewhere in the east of China.
explanation.walkthrough: The radio alphabet is the trick: one letter of the clue is a whole word of the answer, and 'E China' reads as a map reference until it stops. An echo chamber is now the name for any circle that hears only its own opinions coming back.
explanation.definitionFit: An echo chamber returns nothing but what was said into it, which is why the phrase has become the name for a group no dissenting voice reaches.

clue.text: Secret kind of ad

definitions.meaning: the government's word for a paper too sensitive to be let out
the small ads at the back of a paper, sorted into classes — cars, lets, lonely hearts

explanation.surface: An advertisement nobody is supposed to know about.
explanation.walkthrough: Four words are the whole clue because one word is doing both jobs. The small ads are classified in the literal sense of being put into classes, with nothing hidden about them at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Classified means restricted to those cleared to see it, hence secret; and a classified is the categorised small ad the back pages are full of.

clue.text: Daft pedaller is in rope-soled footwear

indicators.note: Somebody daft is not thinking straight, and letters labelled daft are not standing straight either.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A silly cyclist standing about in canvas summer shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' looks like the verb holding the sentence together and is two of the letters. The espadrille is the flat canvas shoe of the Spanish and French Mediterranean, worn everywhere there in summer.
explanation.definitionFit: An espadrille is built on a plaited sole of esparto rope, which is the feature the definition picks out to name it by.

clue.text: Primarily, 'blasted obdurate'; likewise: socialist, hectoring in extremis!

definitions.text: 'blasted obdurate'; likewise: socialist, hectoring in extremis!

indicators.note: What comes primarily comes first, so every word that follows gives up its opening letter and nothing else.

parts.words: blasted obdurate'; likewise: socialist, hectoring in extremis
parts.note: the opening letter of each of the seven words in turn

explanation.surface: A furious description of somebody bloody-minded, left-wing and forever lecturing.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word does two jobs: read straight they describe the person, read down their initials they spell the name for one. Bolshie is short for Bolshevik and in Britain means stroppy as much as left-wing; 'in extremis' is Latin for at the very limit.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: bolshie is the British word for an obstinate, argumentative left-winger, which is what the pile of adjectives adds up to.

clue.text: Lookalikes in nightcaps, maybe

definitions.meaning: a double is the person who could pass for you, the one a film star sends on for the stunts
a nightcap is the last drink of the evening, and a double is a measure of spirits poured twice over

explanation.surface: People who look exactly alike, met over the last drinks of the night.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'maybe' is doing honest work: a nightcap need not be a double, so that half of the clue is a definition by example. Both senses come off the same plain word, which is what keeps the clue to four words.
explanation.definitionFit: A double is somebody's exact likeness, and behind a bar it is the two-measure pour a last drink of the night may well be.

clue.text: Stagger company with ultimately rancid fish

parts.note: a boat that rocks lurches from side to side, and so does a person who staggers
Co is the abbreviation on every firm's letterhead

indicators.note: What comes ultimately comes at the very end, so the word beside it hands over its final letter and nothing more.

parts.note: the last letter of the word, which is what the instruction asked for

explanation.surface: Shocking the firm by serving them fish that has finally gone off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stagger' is the lurching sense here, not the astonishing one the surface is trading on. Rock cod is the market name for the cod-like fish that keep to rocky ground close inshore.
explanation.definitionFit: Rock cod is a food fish of inshore rocky water, so the bare 'fish' names it by the class it belongs to.

clue.text: Perhaps info from spy that's increasingly lazy

definitions.meaning: the bundle of collected material an agent hands over, and 'perhaps' owns that spying is only one place you meet one
doss is British slang for lounging about doing nothing, and -ier is the ending English puts on an adjective to mean more so

explanation.surface: Intelligence handed over by an agent who is getting steadily more bone idle.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is in the ending: a word taken whole from French is read as though English had built it out of an adjective and -ier. To doss is British slang for lounging about doing nothing, though no dictionary carries the adjective this comparative implies.
explanation.definitionFit: A dossier is a file of gathered information, the spy's stock in trade; read the other way it is the comparative of an adjective from doss, British slang for idling.

clue.text: Getting names wrong, Everyman, a kind of absent-mindedness

indicators.note: Getting a thing wrong is getting it out of true, and letters got wrong finish in the wrong order.

parts.note: five letters of fodder
the setter signs himself Everyman, so when he turns up in his own clue he is the first person
the article joins the shuffle as it stands

explanation.surface: The setter owning up to a certain vagueness about who people are.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman means himself whenever his name appears in a clue, and the crossword's first person is a single letter. The definition is generous: amnesia is memory wiped out rather than ordinary woolliness.
explanation.definitionFit: Amnesia is loss of memory, which the clue files under absent-mindedness — the everyday phrase for not having a thing in mind.

clue.text: Swim topless, 'creative work' — truly!

indicators.note: Topless means with the top taken off, and the top of a word in a down entry is the letter it begins with.

parts.note: to bathe is to swim, and the B at the top of the word has gone
art is creative work, put in quotation marks as though somebody doubted it

explanation.surface: Somebody swimming with nothing on top and calling the result art.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks are the setter raising an eyebrow at the claim, and the dash is all that separates wordplay from definition. To be something at heart is to be it underneath everything else.
explanation.definitionFit: What a person is at heart is what they are in their deepest nature, which is the claim 'truly' makes.

clue.text: Flying creature from the red planet, very hard and disappointingly rarer to capture one

indicators.note: A disappointing result is one that has not come out as it should, and letters that have not come out as they should are in a new order.
To capture is to take prisoner and hold inside, so the letters just made close round the one named next.

parts.note: Mars looks red from earth because its dust is full of iron oxide
H is the pencil maker's mark for a hard lead, and the grade above it doubles the letter
the five letters of rarer settled in a new order
one is I in Roman numerals, dropped inside

explanation.surface: A flying thing from Mars, hard to catch and getting rarer every year.
explanation.walkthrough: Pencil grades are where crosswords get H for hard, and a box marked HH is the harder lead again. The marsh harrier is Britain's largest harrier, a wetland hawk that quarters reedbeds on raised wings.
explanation.definitionFit: A marsh harrier is a bird of prey hunting low over the reeds, so 'flying creature' names it by the broadest class it fits.

clue.text: Artist, somewhat sesquipedalian

indicators.note: Somewhat means to some extent and not the whole, so only a stretch of the long word beside it is wanted.

parts.note: four letters running unbroken inside the word, from its ninth letter on

explanation.surface: An artist with a weakness for very long words.
explanation.walkthrough: Sesquipedalian means given to long words and is a long word itself, which is the joke the clue is built on — it comes from the Latin for a foot and a half. Salvador Dalí was the Spanish surrealist of the melting clocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Salvador Dalí was a Spanish surrealist painter, so 'artist' names him by his trade.

clue.text: Notebook entry describes this English county

indicators.note: To describe a circle is to draw round it, so the words in front are drawn around the letters that 'this' points at.

parts.note: the last letter of the first word runs straight on into the first three of the second

explanation.surface: A line jotted in a notebook that happens to describe a county.
explanation.walkthrough: The join between two words is where hidden answers like to sit, because the eye skips over it. Kent is the county at England's south-eastern corner, called the Garden of England for its orchards and hop gardens.
explanation.definitionFit: Kent is one of the historic counties of England, lying between London and the Channel, so the definition names it by kind and country.

clue.text: Somewhere in W Asia — obtained from bazaar — tajine? No thanks …!

indicators.note: Letters obtained from a source come away loose, so they need not arrive in the order that source had them in.
A flat no cancels whatever comes after it, so those letters are struck out before the rest are used.

parts.note: the market of the East, six letters of fodder
a tajine is the North African stew and the conical pot it cooks in; with the TA struck out, four letters remain
ta is the everyday British thanks, and it is what comes out of the stew

explanation.surface: Turning down a stew that somebody picked up at the market.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs the sentence on into the next clue, which is how Everyman ties a pair of them together. Azerbaijan sits on the western shore of the Caspian, and a tajine is North African rather than Asian — the food is misdirection, not geography.
explanation.definitionFit: Azerbaijan lies in the Caucasus between Russia and Iran, which is West Asia by the usual reckoning.

clue.text: … foreign currency in den, from the East

indicators.note: East is the right-hand end of an across entry, so a word arriving from there is read back to front.

parts.note: a den is a lair, an animal's hiding place, and its letters are taken from the back end forwards

explanation.surface: Money from abroad turning up in somebody's hideout.
explanation.walkthrough: This clue picks up the sentence the one before it left hanging, so the opening dots are punctuation rather than instruction. The rial is the money of Iran, Oman and Yemen.
explanation.definitionFit: The rial is the currency of Iran, Oman and Yemen, so from a British paper's desk it is foreign money.

clue.text: Reads hype from Milan footballers: they've come a long way!

parts.note: Internazionale of Milan, founded 1908, are Inter to everyone
PR is public relations, the trade that talks a thing up
an ET is an extra-terrestrial, and any that get here have travelled further than anybody

explanation.surface: Reading the publicity put out by an Italian club that has clearly come a long way.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark is the giveaway: what has come a long way is not the club but the visitors. To interpret a text is to read it in the sense of making out what it means.
explanation.definitionFit: To interpret a poem or a law is to read it — to work out what it is saying — which is the sense 'reads' carries here.

clue.text: Redundant, a false god? So they say

indicators.note: So they say points at what other people's mouths do with the word, so it is the sound that is wanted and not the spelling.

parts.note: an idol is the graven image the commandment calls a false god, and the two spellings sound alike

explanation.surface: Gossip that a fallen idol has been let go.
explanation.walkthrough: Idol and the answer fall together in British speech, which is all the clue needs. Redundant is the British word for a worker whose job has been done away with, and machinery standing unused is idle in the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: Something idle is standing with no work to do, which is what redundant says of a worker or a plant left over.
